title: Knowledge Systems: The New GTM Stack — Jeffrey Wang, Exa

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on rebuilding a company's go-to-market workflow around AI agents and a personal AI clone, with emphasis on org design and how humans collaborate with the system. Primary domain is internal enterprise GTM operations; customer-support-style alerting (Request Lens) and a general-purpose agent platform are also discussed. Exa is running this stack in production across a ~115-person company with active users in Slack and Salesforce MCP. Concepts assume familiarity with ICP/TAM, MCP, CRMs, and coding agents, but no deep research or systems background is required. Single-speaker conference talk (AI Engineer) with live demo and Q&A. Concepts and numbers (e.g., 760 emails, 115 people, 8–9 FDEs, ~dozen agents) are stated directly in the transcript.

summary:
Jeffrey Wang, cofounder of Exa (a web search engine built for AI agents powering Cursor, Cognition, and others), frames go-to-market as an AI engineering problem suited to technical builders. He dismisses the product-versus-distribution debate as settled: a company needs both, and GTM has historically been neglected by engineer-led startups. The central thesis is that GTM is fundamentally a data problem requiring a live model of the world—internal data on customers, product usage, and people, plus external data on 60M+ companies and billions of LinkedIn users—that agents can programmatically act on.

Wang walks through four concrete pieces of Exa's internal GTM stack. The ICP Dashboard uses Exa's web embeddings to classify nearly every company in the total addressable market by category and attach anticipated spend per account (e.g., SpaceX). Request Lens fires alerts when meaningful customer events occur—signups, usage surges, sudden stops. The GTM team runs roughly a dozen coding-style agents inside Slack with broad internal data access, used heavily by account executives for demos and account research. Jeffbot is Wang's personal AI clone: over a week off in Mexico he analyzed 760 of his own emails to derive his voice (averaging 18 words, signing off with "best" not "sincerely"), turned hundreds of past decisions in Slack and email into evals to calibrate judgment, and gave it read/write access to systems he personally uses—so anyone at Exa can ask Jeffbot to draft Slack messages.

He closes with three principles for agent-first companies: agent-first requires API-first because agents cannot reach data without programmatic interfaces (MCP, CLI, or otherwise); not everything should be a chatbot, because consistent learnable UIs still beat generated ones, and crystallized UIs plus flexible chat agents are both important; and buy-versus-build is a false dichotomy—what matters is whether the system is arbitrarily customizable, illustrated by Exa using Salesforce because it's a good database with good opinions, exposed via Salesforce MCP that all their agents use daily. In Q&A Wang explains that Jeffbot, when called by Wang himself, can read and write across many systems, but when called by anyone else at the company it can only draft messages and is restricted from permissions Wang grants himself. He describes the GTM org as AEs, SDRs, and a separate Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) organization of eight to nine people inside a ~115-person company. Non-FDE GTM staff are not vibe coding but are trained to use AI tools well, while FDEs both run/support deals and build/maintain the sales tooling—a single job made possible by AI that previously was two. He credits Palantir for originating the FDE title and frames it as a new model that works well at current scale, though it may not scale to every FDE doing everything.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: GTM is an AI engineering problem engineers should own, not a non-technical afterthought.
The product-vs-distribution debate is settled: you need both to have a company.
GTM is fundamentally a data problem requiring a live model of internal and external world data agents can act on.
Exa's ICP dashboard uses web embeddings to classify nearly every company in the TAM with anticipated spend per account.
Jeffbot was built from 760 personal emails and hundreds of past Slack/email decisions turned into evals to clone Wang's voice and judgment.
Agent-first requires API-first because agents need programmatic interfaces to reach data; Salesforce MCP is used daily by all Exa agents.
Not everything should be a chatbot—crystallized consistent UIs plus flexible chat agents are both needed.
Buy-vs-build is a false dichotomy; the real question is whether the system is arbitrarily customizable, not who built it.
Jeffbot has tiered permissions: full read/write when Wang calls it, draft-only and restricted MCPs when others call it.
Exa's GTM org includes a Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team of 8–9 inside a ~115-person company that both runs deals and builds the sales tooling.

sections.title: Exa and why engineers should care about go-to-market
sections.summary: Wang introduces Exa as a search engine for AI agents powering Cursor and Cognition. He argues engineers should care about GTM, dismisses the product-vs-distribution debate as settled, and reframes GTM as an AI engineering problem—citing X.ai as a place where the team was biased toward building and neglected marketing and sales.

sections.title: Go-to-market is a data problem
sections.summary: Wang lays out the GTM laundry list—researching customers, finding targets, building POCs—and proposes the grand unifying theme: GTM is a data problem requiring a live model of the world that agents can act on, combining internal data (customers, people, product usage) with external data (60M+ companies, billions of LinkedIn users, ongoing news).

sections.title: Two interfaces: ICP dashboard and Request Lens
sections.summary: Wang demos two internal interfaces. The ICP Dashboard uses Exa's web embeddings to classify nearly every company in the TAM by category (model providers, AI coding platforms, GTM intelligence) with anticipated spend per account like SpaceX. Request Lens fires alerts when meaningful customer events occur—signups, usage surges, sudden stops.

sections.title: Two agents: Slack agents and Jeffbot
sections.summary: Wang describes two agent layers. Roughly a dozen coding-style agents run in Slack with broad internal data access, used heavily by GTM staff including AEs building demos. Jeffbot is a personal AI clone he built over a week off in Mexico with Opus 4.5—derived voice from 760 emails (avg 18 words, signs with "best" not "sincerely"), calibrated judgment via evals on hundreds of past decisions, and given read/write access to his systems so anyone at Exa can draft Slack messages in his voice.

sections.title: Three principles for agent-first companies
sections.summary: Wang closes with three principles: agent-first requires API-first because agents need programmatic interfaces to reach internal and external data (via MCP, CLI, or equivalents); not everything should be a chatbot—crystallized consistent UIs plus flexible chat agents are both important; and buy-vs-build is a false dichotomy where the real question is whether the system is arbitrarily customizable, illustrated by Exa using Salesforce because it has good opinions and exposes MCP, which all their agents use daily.

sections.title: Q&A: decision artifacts, GTM team composition, and FDE origins
sections.summary: Asked what artifacts he used for Jeffbot's decision evals, Wang says he mined Slack and email history for hundreds of past decisions. Asked about the GTM team's technical split, he describes AEs, SDRs, and a separate FDE (forward deployed engineering) organization. Non-FDE GTM staff are trained to use AI tools but do not vibe code the interfaces; FDEs both run/support deals and build/maintain the AI tooling. Asked about FDE origins, Wang credits Palantir for the title and frames the role as a new merger of solutions/sales-engineering and AE work that AI now makes possible as a single job.

sections.title: Q&A: security boundaries and org size
sections.summary: Asked about security, Wang explains Jeffbot is tiered: when Wang himself calls it, it has broad read/write access across many systems; when anyone else at Exa calls it, Jeffbot can only draft messages and Wang does not grant it the same MCP permissions. The Q&A closes with the company at about 115 people and the FDE team at eight or nine.

organization.name: Exa
organization.summary: Exa is an independent San Francisco applied-AI search company co-founded by Will Bryk (CEO) and Jeff Wang. First-party pages describe a search API and embeddings built for AI agents, with Search, Contents, Agent, and Monitors products plus an official MCP server. The about page lists Jeff Wang as co-founder and says Exa powers Cursor, Cognition, HubSpot, OpenRouter, Monday.com, and hundreds of thousands of developers. This talk is Wang presenting Exa’s own agent-first GTM system, not a third-party vendor mention.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. Homepage, about, Search product, docs, MCP, and the official JavaScript SDK repo are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
